title: The Car Keys
teaser: Your father, 78, just asked why you're 'suddenly' so interested in whether he still drives at night.
concept: Letting go of the fixed roles 'the parent who decides' and 'the child who obeys' as they quietly reverse.

start.text: "I'm not an idiot," he says, before you've even finished the sentence. "I know why you're asking. You think I can't do this anymore." There's more hurt in his voice than anger, even though it sounds like anger.
start.reflection: Are you trying to protect him, or trying to feel like you've done the responsible thing as his child — and can you tell the difference right now?

choices.label: Lay out the safety concerns plainly, one by one.
"I'm scared of losing you. That's really what this is."

ending_managed.text: He agrees, eventually, to stop driving after dark — but something in the conversation has quietly shifted the ground between you, from two adults to a manager and the managed. It's safer. It's also a little lonelier for both of you.
ending_managed.insight: The sutra's warning about the 'mark of a life-span' — clinging to a fixed story about who someone is across time — applies to roles too. Treating your father only as 'a safety risk to manage' protects him and diminishes him in the same motion.

ending_honest.text: He's quiet for a long moment. "I'm scared of that too," he finally says. The conversation about night driving still needs to happen — it does, a few minutes later — but it happens between two people who are afraid of the same thing, not across a decision being imposed.
ending_honest.insight: Giving him the truth of your fear, without needing to be seen as the responsible one who handled it correctly, let the real conversation — the one under the car keys — actually take place.
